publicationRule: Worked examples illustrate reasoning paths, not universal prescriptions. Keep numerical values contextual, preserve uncertainty, and do not publish an example as an authoritative answer key until independent review is recorded.

examples.title: VPD reading looks acceptable, leaves still show excessive demand
examples.scenario: A room controller reports a VPD inside the facility's preferred operating band, but upper-canopy leaves are curling upward and leaf temperature differs from the controller's assumed value.
reasoningPath: Treat the controller value as a calculated description of the measured air, not proof that every leaf experiences the same vapor-pressure conditions.
Verify the air-temperature and RH sensors, then measure representative leaf temperature and compare multiple canopy positions.
Check airflow, light load, root-zone water status, and duration of the excursion because each can change leaf response without changing the room-average display.
Recalculate leaf-referenced VPD using measured leaf temperature when that is the question being tested.
Change one primary environmental driver at a time where safe, then re-measure both environment and plant response.
evidenceToCollect: air temperature and RH at canopy height
weakAnswerPatterns: The VPD number is in range, so the environment cannot be the cause.
Raise humidity immediately without checking sensor placement or leaf temperature.
Treat one chart band as a universal target for every cultivar and stage.
examples.verification: A stronger conclusion requires representative canopy measurements and a repeatable improvement in plant response after the targeted change, not merely a corrected controller number.
examples.boundary: No universal Cannabis VPD target is implied; cultivar, stage, leaf temperature, disease risk, root status, and measurement method affect interpretation.

examples.title: High center PPFD, weak edge growth
examples.scenario: A grow reports strong PPFD directly under the center of each fixture, yet edge plants stretch and yield less.
reasoningPath: Reject the single-point measurement as a description of whole-canopy light distribution.
Create a repeatable PPFD grid at a defined canopy plane and record fixture height, spacing, dimming, and measurement geometry.
Calculate distribution metrics and inspect the actual minimums/hotspots instead of relying on the average alone.
Compare light pattern with plant height, morphology, leaf temperature, and final zone-by-zone outcomes.
Adjust fixture layout, height, dimming, or canopy geometry only after identifying the spatial problem.
weakAnswerPatterns: The fixture is powerful enough because the center reading is high.
Use one average PPFD value to describe uniformity.
Raise intensity everywhere without checking hotspots.
examples.verification: Repeat the same mapped measurements after the adjustment and compare edge-to-center uniformity plus plant response.
examples.boundary: Uniformity targets depend on crop geometry, fixture design, production goal, and the chosen metric; one map should not be generalized to all rooms.

examples.title: Yellowing appears after a bloom-booster increase
examples.scenario: Lower leaves yellow after phosphorus-heavy bloom inputs are increased. The grower assumes phosphorus deficiency and proposes adding more.
reasoningPath: Separate the visible symptom from the nutrient diagnosis because lower-leaf yellowing is not phosphorus-specific.
Review root-zone pH/EC, irrigation pattern, root condition, recent recipe changes, and the broader symptom distribution.
Check whether the nutrient change increased total ionic strength or antagonism risk rather than assuming the named nutrient is missing.
Compare feed and root-zone context over time instead of interpreting a single runoff value as proof.
Only change the nutrient program after competing root-zone and environmental explanations are evaluated.
evidenceToCollect: feed/root-zone pH and EC with sampling method
weakAnswerPatterns: Yellow lower leaves mean phosphorus deficiency.
More bloom booster is the safest first response.
A single runoff number proves the nutrient cause.
examples.verification: New growth and root-zone trends should improve after the targeted correction without creating a new imbalance.
examples.boundary: This example does not prescribe a phosphorus target or fertilizer rate; diagnosis depends on system, substrate, stage, sampling, and product formulation.

examples.title: One photo is labeled a nutrient deficiency
examples.scenario: A single close-up photo shows yellow and necrotic leaf tissue. The initial claim is 'magnesium deficiency.'
reasoningPath: Describe the symptom before naming the cause: tissue age, location, pattern, progression, and affected fraction.
Request whole-plant and crop-context evidence, then compare affected and unaffected plants.
Inspect roots and irrigation delivery and review pH/EC, environment, recent changes, pests, disease signs, and chemical exposure.
Keep multiple plausible causes until a measurement or sample discriminates among them.
Define what observation after correction would support or weaken the leading hypothesis.
weakAnswerPatterns: Leaf color alone identifies the deficiency.
The most common cause must be correct.
Improvement after several simultaneous changes proves the diagnosis.
examples.verification: A strong diagnosis predicts the spatial/temporal pattern and survives comparison with competing explanations, then is supported by a defined response after a controlled correction.
examples.boundary: Some cases remain multifactorial or unresolved and may require laboratory or specialist confirmation.

examples.title: Recurring pest problem despite calendar sprays
examples.scenario: A facility applies a pesticide on a fixed schedule, but the same pest keeps returning in the same production zone.
reasoningPath: Treat repeated recurrence as a systems problem rather than automatically escalating spray frequency.
Confirm pest identity and life stage, map hotspots, and review intake, movement, sanitation, exclusion, crop residues, and environmental conditions.
Identify which prevention barrier is failing and whether the intervention timing matches pest biology.
Check legal label requirements, resistance-management considerations, and compatibility with biological controls.
Use repeated counts and defined thresholds/tolerances to decide whether the revised program is working.
weakAnswerPatterns: Spray more often because the product did not work.
Seeing fewer adults once proves control.
IPM is just rotating pesticides.
examples.verification: The revised program should reduce pest pressure over repeated scouting intervals while preserving compliance and preventing the same pathway from reseeding the problem.
examples.boundary: No pesticide, threshold, release rate, or treatment interval is prescribed here; lawful use depends on current labels, jurisdiction, crop context, and facility policy.

examples.title: Small F2 population misses a rare trait combination
examples.scenario: A breeder expects to recover several independent favorable traits in an F2 but only grows a small population and finds none.
reasoningPath: Translate the desired phenotype into an explicit genetic/trait model instead of assuming one plant should appear by chance.
Estimate how trait number, linkage, dominance, recombination, penetrance, and scoring error affect recovery probability.
Set population size from the probability of the desired combination and the need for multiple independent candidates.
Preserve all scored classes and environmental context so absence can be interpreted rather than hidden by selection.
Revise the population design if the probability of recovery was too low for the chosen sample size.
weakAnswerPatterns: No selected plant means the trait combination is impossible.
A small F2 is enough if the parents are strong.
Only the best plants need to be recorded.
examples.verification: A defensible conclusion compares observed counts with a predeclared model and acknowledges when population size cannot distinguish rarity from absence.
examples.boundary: Simple Mendelian probabilities apply only when the underlying assumptions are justified; quantitative traits and linkage can change expected recovery sharply.

examples.title: New meter shows more decimal places
examples.scenario: A replacement meter displays two decimal places instead of one, and the team concludes that measurements are now more accurate.
reasoningPath: Separate display resolution from accuracy, precision, repeatability, bias, and uncertainty.
Check manufacturer specifications, calibration/verification records, reference standards, and repeat measurements.
Compare the instrument against a suitable reference across the actual operating range.
Document as-found condition and any adjustment rather than assuming calibration erases all uncertainty.
Report only the digits justified by method performance and decision needs.
weakAnswerPatterns: More decimal places always mean more accuracy.
A recent calibration guarantees every future result.
Repeat readings close together prove the result is true.
examples.verification: The instrument must meet predefined acceptance criteria against appropriate references and demonstrate suitable repeatability over the intended range.
examples.boundary: Measurement uncertainty is method- and use-specific; this example does not establish a universal tolerance.

examples.title: One sensor is used to represent an entire room
examples.scenario: A cultivation room uses one centrally located sensor to support a claim that all plants experienced the same temperature and RH.
reasoningPath: Define the population and decision: whether the claim concerns the whole room, canopy zones, time periods, or a specific crop operation.
Identify likely spatial and temporal gradients created by fixtures, walls, doors, airflow, irrigation, and canopy density.
Choose representative sampling locations and times before collecting the data.
Distinguish repeated readings from one sensor from independent spatial samples.
Use the resulting variation to decide whether one fixed sensor is representative enough for the intended decision.
weakAnswerPatterns: A central sensor automatically represents the room.
Many readings from one location equal many independent samples.
An average proves there were no harmful extremes.
examples.verification: A representative plan should reproduce the important spatial and temporal variation well enough to support the stated decision, with limits documented.
examples.boundary: Sampling density depends on room geometry, variability, equipment, risk, and the consequence of missing extremes.

examples.title: Root decline after repeated wet irrigation
examples.scenario: Plants in one irrigation zone lose vigor and develop brown roots after a period of frequent irrigation. The first assumption is that a root pathogen is definitely responsible.
reasoningPath: Treat brown roots and poor vigor as evidence of root decline, not proof of a particular pathogen.
Compare affected and unaffected plants from the same cohort and map whether the problem follows an irrigation zone, media lot, cultivar, or propagation source.
Measure root-zone moisture, drainage, temperature, EC, irrigation timing, and oxygen-related context before interpreting pathogen tests.
Inspect roots for lesion pattern and sample early symptomatic tissue when laboratory confirmation is warranted.
Keep abiotic predisposition, pathogen involvement, and mixed causes in the differential until the spatial pattern, root-zone data, and diagnostic evidence agree.
evidenceToCollect: laboratory or microscopy results when used
weakAnswerPatterns: Brown roots prove Pythium or another single pathogen.
Wet media alone proves disease.
Finding one organism means root-zone stress no longer matters.
examples.verification: A stronger conclusion requires the proposed cause to match the crop pattern and root findings, and the corrective plan should improve new root and shoot growth while repeat measurements show the predisposing condition or confirmed disease pressure has changed.
examples.boundary: Root disease severity depends on organism, host, media, water status, temperature, sanitation, and sampling. This example does not establish a universal irrigation frequency or pathogen diagnosis.

examples.title: A dryback percentage is copied from another facility
examples.scenario: A grow adopts a dryback percentage from an online chart but has different containers, substrate, sensor placement, irrigation frequency, and plant size.
reasoningPath: Define exactly what the percentage represents: volumetric water content, sensor output, container mass, or another reference.
Document the starting reference point and the time interval so the reported dryback is reproducible.
Compare sensor position and substrate heterogeneity before assuming one reading represents the whole root zone.
Interpret the change alongside plant demand, root-zone EC, irrigation volume, drainage, environment, and crop stage.
Use controlled adjustments and plant response to establish a local operating range instead of copying one percentage as a universal target.
evidenceToCollect: sensor position or container mass method
weakAnswerPatterns: A specific dryback percentage is ideal for every setup.
Sensor percentage and water-content percentage are automatically interchangeable.
More dryback always improves root health.
examples.verification: A useful local dryback strategy should produce repeatable water-status trends, acceptable root-zone chemistry, and stable plant response across representative plants rather than merely matching a borrowed number.
examples.boundary: Dryback values are method-, substrate-, container-, sensor-, plant-, and climate-specific; this example does not prescribe a universal percentage.

examples.title: Clone matches genotype but performs differently
examples.scenario: A cutting from a favored mother is genetically expected to match the donor, but the clone grows poorly after rooting and the team concludes it must have genetically changed.
reasoningPath: Separate inherited genotype from biological state; a cutting normally preserves genotype but also carries age, pathogen status, epigenetic state, reserves, and handling history.
Verify donor identity and chain of propagation before invoking genetic change.
Compare rooting quality, sanitation, environment, root-zone conditions, and source-plant health.
Consider whether disease, physiological stress, or propagation conditions explain the performance difference.
Use genetic testing only when the question truly concerns identity or sequence variation rather than as a substitute for horticultural diagnosis.
evidenceToCollect: genotype/fingerprint data if identity is uncertain
weakAnswerPatterns: A clone must perform identically because the DNA is the same.
Poor clone performance proves a mutation.
Genetic identity testing explains every performance difference.
examples.verification: If identity is confirmed, the explanation should be tested against propagation and health evidence; improvement after correcting those factors supports a physiological or management cause more strongly than an unsupported mutation claim.
examples.boundary: Clonal propagation preserves inherited genotype under normal conditions but does not guarantee identical phenotype, health, vigor, or epigenetic state across environments and propagation histories.

examples.title: Dense flower rot is assumed to be Botrytis
examples.scenario: Brown internal tissue and gray material are found inside dense flowers late in production. The crop team immediately labels the case Botrytis without collecting a diagnostic sample.
reasoningPath: Describe the affected tissue, distribution, progression, and visible signs before assigning the pathogen.
Inspect nearby flowers and environmental history for prolonged wetness, condensation, injuries, senescent tissue, and canopy microclimates.
Compare the appearance with other fungal, bacterial, insect, and abiotic causes of flower breakdown.
Collect representative early-stage symptomatic tissue when confirmation affects disposition or management.
Separate containment and sanitation actions from the final causal claim so risk can be reduced while diagnosis remains appropriately qualified.
weakAnswerPatterns: Any gray or brown flower rot is Botrytis.
High humidity proves Botrytis infection.
A photo alone establishes pathogen identity.
examples.verification: Diagnostic confidence increases when characteristic signs, disease pattern, environmental context, and laboratory or microscopic evidence converge; follow-up should show whether containment and environmental corrections reduce new cases.
examples.boundary: Visible flower rot can have multiple causes. This example does not define a universal humidity threshold or replace laboratory confirmation when pathogen identity matters.

examples.title: Drying room setpoint is stable but batches dry unevenly
examples.scenario: A drying room holds a stable temperature and RH, yet flowers at different rack positions finish at very different times.
reasoningPath: Treat the room setpoint as an input, not proof of uniform product conditions.
Map rack position, load density, obstructions, fan paths, and return-air locations.
Measure representative air and product conditions across the load rather than only at the controller.
Track mass loss or other validated drying indicators by position over time.
Adjust loading, spacing, airflow, or room operation based on the observed distribution, then repeat the same spatial measurements.
evidenceToCollect: final moisture or water activity where appropriate
weakAnswerPatterns: Stable room RH means every product zone dries equally.
One controller sensor describes the entire load.
The slowest zone only needs more time; spatial airflow does not matter.
examples.verification: The adjustment should reduce position-dependent differences in drying curves and final product condition when measured with the same sampling plan.
examples.boundary: Drying behavior depends on product geometry, load, airflow, equipment, temperature, RH, and sampling. No single room setting guarantees uniformity.

examples.title: One phenotype wins in one room
examples.scenario: A breeding candidate outperforms siblings in one room and is immediately declared genetically superior.
reasoningPath: Define the trait and measurement method before interpreting the apparent advantage.
Identify position, room, season, management, and measurement factors that could explain the result.
Use replication and appropriate randomization or blocking to separate candidate effects from environmental noise.
Include checks or reference genotypes when possible and preserve all observations rather than only selected winners.
Retest the candidate across relevant environments before converting one result into a stable genetic claim.
weakAnswerPatterns: Best in one room means genetically best.
Many measurements from one plant equal biological replication.
A strong phenotype automatically has high breeding value.
examples.verification: A genetic-performance claim becomes stronger when the advantage repeats across independent experimental units or environments and remains after accounting for known spatial or management effects.
examples.boundary: Replication requirements depend on the trait, population, environmental variability, and decision risk; one trial cannot establish universal performance.

examples.title: Testing two irrigation strategies without pseudoreplication
examples.scenario: A grow wants to compare two irrigation strategies but assigns one whole room to Strategy A and another room to Strategy B, then treats every plant as an independent replicate.
reasoningPath: Define the experimental unit as the smallest unit independently assigned to treatment.
Recognize that if treatment is assigned by room, plants within the same room are subsamples rather than independent treatment replicates.
Identify room-level confounders such as fixtures, airflow, staff practice, cultivar distribution, and equipment.
Redesign with independent replicated treatment units, randomization, or a defensible blocked/crossover structure where operationally possible.
Predefine outcomes and analysis before seeing the results.
weakAnswerPatterns: Twenty plants in one treated room equal twenty treatment replicates.
A difference between two rooms proves the irrigation treatment caused it.
More subsamples fix missing independent replication.
examples.verification: The experiment supports stronger causal inference when treatments are independently replicated and competing room or position effects are controlled or estimated rather than perfectly confounded with treatment.
examples.boundary: Operational cultivation trials may require blocking or staged designs; the correct experimental unit depends on how treatment is actually applied.

examples.title: Higher light is correlated with higher yield
examples.scenario: Historical production data show that crops with higher measured light also had higher yield, and the team concludes that increasing light caused the yield increase.
reasoningPath: Confirm temporal order and how both light and yield were measured.
List variables that changed with light, including cultivar, plant density, CO2, nutrition, crop age, room, season, and management.
Distinguish confounders from mediators and from consequences of the treatment.
Use a controlled or quasi-experimental comparison when a causal claim matters.
Phrase the historical result as an association unless the design rules out credible alternative explanations.
weakAnswerPatterns: Correlation proves the higher light caused the yield change.
A statistically strong relationship cannot be confounded.
Adding more variables after seeing the result automatically establishes causality.
examples.verification: A causal interpretation becomes more credible when treatment precedes outcome, assignment or design reduces confounding, measurements are comparable, and alternative explanations fail to account for the observed effect.
examples.boundary: Observational cultivation data are valuable for hypothesis generation and forecasting but often cannot support causal claims without additional design or analysis.
